newsitem.title: USA: Economic insecurity fails to work for Dole.
newsitem.headline: Economic insecurity fails to work for Dole.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Republican Bob Dole counted on the economic insecurity of voters to boost his campaign, but a Reuters poll shows President Bill Clinton is stronger even among people who fear unemployment or recently lost a job.
The poll of 1,019 likely voters conducted by the John Zogby Group found a significant amount of economic insecurity in the nation despite the generally healthy economy.

Nearly 11 percent of respondents said they or someone in their household lost a job in the past year. An additional 15 percent said they or a member of their household feared losing a job in the next year. And 19 percent said they or a member of their household were working for less money than in an immediate previous job.
These people ought to be fertile ground for Dole, who has promised an across-the-board 15 percent income tax cut and numerous other tax breaks. But they are not.

More than 52 percent of those who said they feared losing their jobs support Clinton versus 31 percent for Dole. For those who had lost their jobs, the figures were almost identical: Clinton 52 percent, Dole 35 percent. For those working for less money, it was Clinton 49 percent, Dole 35.

In the latest piece of good economic news for Clinton, the Labour Department reported that unemployment dropped to 5.1 percent last month from 5.5 percent in July, its lowest level in more than seven years.
"The American economy, my fellow Americans, is on the right track," Clinton said in a speech to a gathering of black religious leaders in Orlando, Florida.
Dole has been unable to capitalise on existing economic insecurity because people fear their plight would only worsen under Republican rule.
"I prefer Clinton because he's not going to let the welfare system just throw everyone out," said Jim Tennington, a bartender from West Virginia who took part in the poll.

Shari Salsburg, a homemaker in Polock Pines, California, whose family has no health insurance, sees Clinton as her best hope for better times. "We're lower middle class. We pay our taxes. But the Republicans in Congress are out for the rich and not for people like us," she said.
The Reuters poll showed Clinton leading Dole overall by 15 percentage points, 48 to 33 percent. Independent Ross Perot trailed with 6 percent.
Three other polls Thursday produced similar results:
-- A CNN/USA Today poll of likely voters had Clinton 17 points ahead.
-- A New York Times poll had Clinton 14 points ahead among likely voters.
-- An ABC/Washington Post poll put the president's lead over Dole at 11 points.

In the last 12 presidential elections, the maximum change in the gap between candidates in the final two months of the campaign was 13 points, achieved by President Harry Truman in 1948. In 1968, Hubert Humphrey fought back from a 12-point September deficit to come within a point of victory against Richard Nixon.

While Clinton leads Dole in most sections of the population, his advantage is a shaky two points among whites and he trails narrowly among Protestants. But he has a huge lead of 50 points among Hispanics, he has 75 percent of the black vote and three quarters of the Jewish vote and he leads by 20 points in the crucial swing Catholic population. He leads by 20 points among women.
The president's base appears rock solid. Almost 85 percent of Democrats and 53 percent of independents as well as 14 percent of Republicans say he deserves re-election.
Even among those describing themselves as conservative, 35 percent said the president deserves a second term.
